original: I heard the story of myself again last night, told across a crowded taproom by a man who had no notion he was telling it to the one it belonged to, and I have been turning it over ever since, the way you turn a stone you picked up without meaning to and now cannot quite bring yourself to set down.

snip: I did not know him, the man in the story. That is the plain truth of it, and plain truth is very nea
original: I did not know him, the man in the story. That is the plain truth of it, and plain truth is very near all I have left that is worth the giving. They have made me into someone in those tales: a figure, a wonder, a man who walked through the whole of his life already knowing the shape of it. And the man they have made is, if I may say so of my own legend, a bit of an ass. Sure of himself. Untouched by anything. Always the right word ready on his lips and never a wrong night lying behind him. I would not cross a room to shake his hand, and I have yet to hear the tale told in a way that made me wish I would.

snip: I had never meant to stay in it long, for that matter. Coming home to my father's house was to be a
original: I had never meant to stay in it long, for that matter. Coming home to my father's house was to be a stopgap and nothing grander, a place to keep myself and my boots while my own house went up across the river; and my own was to be a wonder, or a warning, depending on which of us you asked about it afterward: grander than anything my father would have put his name to, taller, flashier, altogether more foolish, the same clean lines he had given my mother swollen to twice the scale and three times the cost, a great bright thing built to stand as a gift and a grand gesture ahead of a wedding. I had drawn a good part of it myself, in the good years, when I still supposed I knew what I was building toward. There was no wedding, in the end, and so no need of the house. I never lived in it. For three years it had stood across the water full of a life that had not happened, costing me a small fortune a year in the bare keeping of a grand thing that nobody used, and I could no more sell it than cross its threshold. Penworth had spent the better part of that winter trying, with a delicacy that cost him something to keep up, to talk me round to letting it go, for the sake of my purse and, though he was too careful a man to say it, for the sake of the rest of me; and I had spent the winter not answering him. What I had not understood, riding up that valley, was that he had quietly stopped waiting on my answer. Somewhere in the thaw he had found a buyer for it, a real one, ready to close come the spring, and had breathed not a word of that in his letter. He had offered me a hill instead, and asked only, in that mild and immovable way of his, that I come and look at the thing before he let me finish the buying of it. I had given him a yes to the looking and no better than half a yes to the rest, and half a yes was all Penworth had ever needed of me. He knew his man: give me some fresh thing to say yes to, and somewhere sensible for the money to go, and the house I could not make myself sell might at last consent to be sold out from under me while I stood in a far green field admiring a hill. The errand was the lever of it, though he would have been far too tidy a man ever to call it so. I did not much mind being pried loose. I was tired, and it was spring, and a man has to be sent somewhere. I would as soon it were a hill.

snip: The first and easier part of it I had come by rail: three days out of Vethmark in a carriage that ra
original: The first and easier part of it I had come by rail: three days out of Vethmark in a carriage that rattled the teeth in a man's head and let the cold in at every seam. The railways were new then, and it showed. The engine that hauled us was an early, soot-breathing thing, all iron and steam and appetite, and there was next to nothing of the arcane in it, which surprised the sort of people who supposed a wizard must approve of a train on principle. I did not, particularly. You may put a working into a machine, and I have put a good many into a good many; but a working has to be fed and tended and coaxed and renewed, and one big enough to shoulder a train up a grade would have eaten more in the keeping than the coal it saved. Magic in this world does not come by the ton. It comes by the thimble, and dearly, and no sane man spends a thimble of it where a shovelful of coal will serve. So the railways ran on fire and water and brute iron cleverness and almost no magic at all, and I spent a fair part of those three days watching the engine hiss and labor at the watering-stops and thinking, in the idle, itching way of a man who cannot let a made thing alone, how much smaller and quieter and cleverer the whole of it could have been built, if the world had only had the magic to spare for it. It did not. It never has. That is the first hard fact of my trade, and the trains were a great smoking monument to it: a mountain of crude iron doing loudly and dearly what a very little good artifice could have done well, had there only been enough good artifice to go around, which there was not, and is not, and I have stopped expecting there ever to be.

snip: The inn stood where the street widened toward the beck. It was a broad, comfortable-looking building
original: The inn stood where the street widened toward the beck. It was a broad, comfortable-looking building of three storeys, one of the few in Ardenmoor to stand so tall, with a painted sign gone too weathered to read and lamplight already spilling out of its windows into the blue evening. I have stopped at a great many inns and could write a dull and honest book on the subject. This one, before I had so much as got down off my horse, had the one quality that matters and cannot be built on purpose: it looked like somewhere a tired man might stop being tired for a while. I got down, and my legs told me at length exactly how far we had come. A boy came out of the inn-yard shadows to take Snow's head with the unhurried competence of a child who has been around horses since before he could walk.

snip: "You'll be the wizard, then," she said, not loudly, setting down in front of me a cup I had not aske
original: "You'll be the wizard, then," she said, not loudly, setting down in front of me a cup I had not asked for and immediately wanted. She said the word the way another woman might have said *the man about the drains*: a trade like any other, come to do a thing that wanted doing. I have been announced in grander rooms with a great deal more ceremony and a great deal less competence. "Room's held and paid, a fortnight since, by your man's man. Sit. Eat." A glance took the whole of the road off me in one pass. "You've the look of a man who's been eating out of his saddlebags a week."

snip: Cael came in on the tail of the meal, the cold of the evening still on his shoulders and his grandso
original: Cael came in on the tail of the meal, the cold of the evening still on his shoulders and his grandson at his heel. He was not the man I had built out of Penworth's correspondence; I had made him older and grander in my head, and he was a solid man on the near side of old, not young but a fair way yet from grey, in a good plain coat, with a face that had done a great deal of weather in its time and a pair of eyes that had lost none of their sharpness to it. He looked me over the way you look at a thing you have been expecting for months and are pleased, on the whole, to find is real. His glance caught a moment on my face, as people's often did, and came up a good way short of my true count of years. I was past forty by then, and have never worn it where a man can see, for reasons I will come to. Whatever figure he settled on he kept to himself, which I liked him for.

snip: There was no thread of fate in it, whatever a story would want. I did not come to Ardenmoor drawn by
original: There was no thread of fate in it, whatever a story would want. I did not come to Ardenmoor drawn by anything grander than an errand. I came because Penworth had an unerring eye and I had learned to trust it over my own; because it was spring, and I had spent the whole of the winter shut up in a quiet Vethmark townhouse with the spare rooms closed and sheeted, keeping well out of the way of the noise and the standing crowd of small obligations that a city presses on a man whether he asks for them or not, and had barely marked the season going by; and because there was nowhere else in the wide world I would rather have been, which in those days was less a boast than a fairly bleak measure of how small my life had got. *A hill of no worth and considerable quiet.* When I read that, it sounded like very nearly the only thing left that I wanted.
revised: There was no thread of fate in it, whatever a story would want. I did not come to Ardenmoor drawn by anything grander than an errand. I came because Penworth had an unerring eye and I had learned to trust it as if it was my own; because it was spring, and I had spent the whole of the winter shut up in a quiet Vethmark townhouse with the spare rooms closed and sheeted, keeping well out of the way of the noise and the standing crowd of small obligations that a city presses on a man whether he asks for them or not, and had barely marked the season going by; and because there was nowhere else in the wide world I would rather have been, which in those days was less a boast than a fairly bleak measure of how small my life had got. *A hill of no worth and considerable quiet.* When I read that, it sounded like very nearly the only thing left that I wanted.

original: "I made it a fine hill with a fine view," I said, "and a great deal too much quiet to leave alone. I mean to build on it."
revised: "It is a perfectly fine hill with a fine view," I said, "and a great deal too much quiet to leave alone. I would build on it.”

snip: We walked the whole of it, that afternoon, the long slow way round, the way you walk a thing you mea
original: We walked the whole of it, that afternoon, the long slow way round, the way you walk a thing you mean to be answerable for. Cael went at the pace his knees allowed and I was glad of it, because it was the right pace for the ground, slow enough to see. He showed me the spring that came up cold and clear out of the hill's south face and had never once, in living memory or his grandmother's, gone dry; a thing worth more than the hill on top of it, he said, and he was right, and I would have cause to bless that spring a hundred times in the years after. He showed me the woodland strip, good mixed timber, oak and ash and a stand of larch a former owner had planted and not lived to cut. He showed me where the grade eased along the eastern slope into a shelf of deeper, greener grass, and I felt something about that shelf that I had not the knowledge yet to name and did not mention, and Cael did not mention it either, though I caught him watching me not mention it. And all the while the boy Soren went ahead of us and to the side, quiet as weather, stopping now and then to crouch over some particular patch of ground with the total absorption of a child at his real work, and once, near the crown, he stood for a long moment with his bare hand flat on a stone, and then took it off, and came on, and said nothing, and I thought nothing of it, which is a thing I would give a good deal to go back and un-think.

snip: And there is this, besides. Once in a great while, in some inn a long way from anywhere, I will hear
original: And there is this, besides. Once in a great while, in some inn a long way from anywhere, I will hear a story told that I half recognize, the way you might recognize your own coat on a stranger three sizes too large for it. There are not many of them. I am not, whatever you may have been led to expect, a man they sing about; I took a good deal of quiet care, over the years, that it should stay so. But a few tales got loose all the same, and time and retelling have warped them so far out of true that the man in them is half myth and half plain nonsense, and I would not know him to nod to in the road, and, if I am honest, do not much care for him. I hold the tellers no grudge; a good story is a kind of coin, and it is meant to be spent. It only seems a poor thing to leave nothing behind but those few, and so, if only so that the truth of it should exist somewhere, in one place, I mean to set down what actually happened. Or near enough. I will not pretend the years have warmed no words nor softened any faces; fondness does that, and I was fond of very nearly all of them, and they are gone now, every one of them, but me. Still, the shape of it is true, and the shape is the thing that matters.

original: I will not pretend the years have warmed no words or softened no faces in the telling, for I was fond of very nearly all of them. But the shape of it is true, and the shape is the thing that lasts. So here it is, the true version, or near enough: how a hill that nothing would stand on came at last to hold a tower, and how the man who built it there got, without ever quite meaning to, a life back.
